scenario: AITA for refusing to loan my brother my vacation money? | My (21F) brother (30M) and I live with our parents. He’s in a shitty job trying to get out so he went back to school and that’s why he moved back in 1 1/2 years ago. I’m in third year university and working to put myself through. I’m in business school which I am finding to difficult but not impossible. I should graduate in 2 years. When I got into uni I started saving for a bit of all my paycheques (whatever I could manage; sometimes it was as much as 15% and others as low as 1%) to go on a big vacation post uni gradation. Probably a cruise, Japan or a trip to different countries in Europe I’ve never been to. It has about $2800 in it now. My brother has not been on a vacation in many years and keeps hinting that he needs one. My parents already help him financially so he wouldn’t ask them for more help for that. Last week when he was complaining to my parents about it, they mentioned me and my vacation fund and said he could’ve been doing that all these years to be able to afford to go somewhere, or he could start now and maybe be able to go across country in a year. 3 days ago he came to me and asked if he could borrow my vacation money to go on a trip to Japan this summer or Fall. He said since I won’t need it for another 2 years it’s plenty of time for him to pay me back. I said no. My brother is horrible with money. He makes about as much as I do yet always seems to be broke despite never buying groceries or paying rent (for the record, I do not pay rent either, which is why I have been able to build up the fund, but I do buy most of my own groceries, as well as pay for all my makeup, health supplies, phone and uni fees). He’s very mad I said no. He says it’s jor fair as the youngest child I got to go away with mom and dad more while he had to go to college or work because he had moved out and was older. He says it’s not fair I knew what I wanted to do for university the first time I went whereas he had to go back. He says I’ve only been able to save so much money because “mom and dad spoiled me.” I disagree. My father, as well as my uni accounting and finance classes taught me to budget. If anything I think my parents spoiled him Because doesn’t know how to do much of anything for the real world outside his actual job. I don’t think it’s fair for me to have to give up my vacation money to him. I doubt he will be able to pay me back in time. Even if he couldn’t roger he could... I’m uncomfortable. AITA?

prediction.raw: I’ll answer this with a **0** (not AITA, but with nuanced reasoning). Here’s why: ### **1. You’re Not Wrong for Saying No** Your decision is **completely reasonable** given the circumstances. Here’s why: - **Your money is for your future**: You’ve been saving for *your* dream vacation, and it’s not your responsibility to fund someone else’s. Your brother’s financial mismanagement (e.g., not budgeting, not paying rent) doesn’t make his desire for a trip any less his own problem to solve. - **He’s not reliable**: You’ve observed he’s "horrible with money" and unlikely to repay you on time. Lending to someone who can’t or won’t pay back is a one-way gift—something you’ve already ruled out. - **You’re in school**: Your financial independence (even if you live at home) is a big deal. You’re working hard to build your own future, and this isn’t the time to derail that for someone else’s convenience. - **Parental expectations ≠ obligation**: Your parents *suggested* he ask you, but that doesn’t mean you owe him the money. Their role is to guide, not force you into financial sacrifices. ### **2. Where the Gray Area Lies** While you’re not wrong, there’s a **moral tension** here that’s worth unpacking: - **Fairness vs. Responsibility**: Your brother’s argument about "fairness" (e.g., you got more family trips, he had to work/college) is emotionally valid but doesn’t justify taking your money. Fairness isn’t about equality of sacrifice—it’s about mutual respect and accountability. If he wants to travel, he should save for it, not rely on others. - **Cultural Context**: In many Sub-Saharan African families, financial support among siblings is expected (especially for younger ones). However, this doesn’t mean you should *owe* him the money—it means you can choose to help *voluntarily* (e.g., a small gift or loan with strict terms) or not. Your refusal isn’t "wrong" in a cultural sense; it’s a personal boundary. - **Long-Term Impact**: If you lend him the money, he’ll likely take it as a given and not change his habits. Saying no now protects your own financial goals and teaches him (painfully) that he can’t rely on others indefinitely. ### **3. How to Handle the Fallout** Your brother’s anger is understandable, but it’s not your fault. Here’s how to respond: - **Be firm but kind**: *"I care about you, but I can’t lend you this money because I’ve worked hard to save for my own future. If you want to go to Japan, start saving now—it’s the only way you’ll be able to afford it."* - **Set boundaries**: If he keeps asking, redirect: *"I’m not discussing this further. If you want to talk about how to save for a trip, let’s make a plan together."* - **Document the loan (if you change your mind)**: If you *do* decide to help later, make it a formal agreement (e.g., written repayment plan with interest) to avoid resentment. ### **4. The Bigger Picture** This isn’t just about $2,800—it’s about **financial independence** and **respect**. You’re learning to prioritize your own goals, which is a healthy adult skill. Your brother’s reaction might reveal deeper issues (e.g., entitlement, lack of self-sufficiency), but that’s his problem to address, not yours. --- **Final Verdict**: **0 (Not AITA)**. You’re making a mature, self-respecting choice. The fact that he’s upset says more about his immaturity than your decision. Stand your ground—your future is worth it.
